chapter_theme: In the closing verses of the Release sarukkam, the lord guards the fortress of the self, mounts the elephant of knowledge, draws the sword of meditation, kills the karmic enemies one by one, throws the sword away, enters the city of no return and becomes the crest-jewel of the world, while the gods worship and the princes of the story rule on.

cast.role: the unnamed lord who fights karma as a war and wins release; the verses do not name him
the karmic enemy kings and their host
the gods who shower and praise
Prajapati, who rules the Brahma world in 2128
Tirumal of the discus, who rules the earth in 2128 and 2129
the one white as a conch who worships in 2130
the one with a jewel-blue body who worships in 2130
Death and Desire, who flee in 2127

2111.reading: The lord is shown raising a fortress of the self: three rich walls, five sense-gates shut with golden doors, a knowing mind set inside, and twelve faultless ones stationed as guards.
2111.nuance: The verse never says what the three walls or the twelve guards stand for; the allegory is read from the five gates (பொறி, the senses) alone, so the sense of the numbers is left open.
2111.event: The hero builds a walled fortress with its five gates shut and posts twelve faultless guards.

claims.claim: shutting the five sense-gates and guarding the mind is the first defence in the fight against karma

2112.reading: Ten guards stand outside the walls and twelve serve inside, and the lord, wishing to bring his three worlds under one road, sends his force out against the thinning host of the karmic enemy kings.
2112.nuance: The numbers ten and twelve are given without their referents.
2112.event: The hero stations his guards and marches out against the army of the karmic enemies.

claims.claim: liberation is won by a campaign against the army of karma

2113.reading: Having gained four kinds of discipline, the lord mounts the splendid elephant of knowledge, driven by a diamond goad that is awareness itself and kept on the path of the sacred texts and the mind.
2113.nuance: The four named in line 1 (பின்னணி, யோகு, நான்மை, அபரகாத்திரம்) are partly unclear words, and the clause about the texts and the mind in line 2 may be read two ways, so only the picture of knowledge as an elephant under a goad is kept.
2113.event: The hero climbs the elephant of knowledge, steering it with the goad of awareness.

claims.claim: awareness is the goad that drives knowledge along the right path toward the enemy

2114.reading: Driving the great elephant to break the guard of the proud fort, he rides it up a ridge of good qualities, crushes the shape of desire, drives off the outposts of the senses and attacks the stronghold where the karmic enemies live.
2114.event: The hero storms the fort of the karmic enemies on his elephant, crushing desire and the outposts of the senses.

claims.claim: desire and the senses are outposts of the karmic enemy that must be cleared before its stronghold falls

2115.reading: Unable to bear the enemy's unrestraint, he draws the sword of unending meditation, steeped in the water of samadhi, while women suited to the twelve faultless ones fan him with whisks.
2115.nuance: The fanning women are the twelve faultless ones in female form as far as the grammar of line 2 shows, but the verse does not say it outright.
2115.event: The hero draws the sword of meditation while attendants fan him.

claims.claim: unbroken meditation soaked in samadhi is the sword that cuts karma

2116.reading: Serving as the means against the fierce enemies, the lord crushes a group of fierce karmas, razes the sixteen walled forts he has already named, and eight strike down the chieftains.
2116.nuance: Lines 2 and 3 count karmas and forts (seven, sixteen) and line 4 an eight; the verse itself gives no key, and the words கொண்கடா and எண்கடா are hard.
2116.event: The hero and eight of his men break the enemy's forts and cut down its chieftains.

claims.claim: the fierce karmas fall to meditation's attack in a fixed order of forts

2117.reading: With anger and its fellows (eight in all) struck down, a neuter figure leaps into the fire and dies, then a woman falls, six attendants die, and last the man himself sinks after a while.
2117.nuance: The neuter, woman and man with six attendants may be the nine minor passions of the Jain list, but the verse names them only as figures; I follow the picture and not that list.
2117.event: A run of enemy figures led by anger dies in sequence: the neuter, the woman, six attendants and the man.

claims.claim: anger and the passions linked to it are killed one after another in the battle against karma

2118.reading: Four more enemies fall in turn, one of them rising as a half-corpse that is cut down again, and two others who shake the sleeping die as well.
2118.nuance: The grouping of the four and the two, and the sense of the half-corpse, cannot be fixed from the verse.
2118.event: Four enemies fall one by one, and two more die with them.

2119.reading: After those fall, two kings and four more are struck and beheaded, and the lord takes the whole treasure of infinite knowledge and becomes the single master of all the raised-up worlds.
2119.event: The hero kills the last enemy kings, takes the treasure of infinite knowledge and rules all the worlds.

claims.claim: when the enemy kings of karma fall, infinite knowledge is gained and the soul becomes lord of all the worlds

2120.reading: Having reduced four old enemies to ash, he ends the fierce karma; the verse then speaks of the woman called முடிவு, whom he reaches, while gods and kings gather in a host.
2120.nuance: முடிவு (end, completion) is spoken of as a woman in lines 2 and in the verses that follow, so the end of karma is both a deed and a person to be won; the grammar of lines 2 and 3 is hard and the clause is read loosely.
2120.event: The hero reduces four long-standing enemies to ash and ends the karma that bound him.

claims.claim: four deeply rooted karmas are burned to ash before the soul reaches its end

2121.reading: Flags, umbrellas, whisks, the crowns of the gods, their women and their jewels press so close that there is no place left for a foot, and the whole sky is mixed with flowers, sandal and powder.
2121.event: The gods crowd the sky with their regalia and rain flowers, sandal and powder.

2122.reading: The gods scatter gold-threaded garlands, flower-rain honey, pearl strings and jewelled wreaths and praise the lord who cut the crowd of enemies and sits in glory.
2122.event: The gods shower garlands and praise the lord who cut the enemy host.

claims.claim: the one who cut the throng of karma is worthy of the gods' praise

2123.reading: Having wiped out the king of dark karma and wanting the princess called the Lord's end without parting, he enters a rich city from which none returns even after the ages turn.
2123.nuance: Line 1 is corrupt (கருமால் வினையரசு காறளர நூறிப்து) and the third line's வேட்டு எய்தி may mean wedding the woman called முடிவு or merely winning her; the sense of the destroyed king is kept, the details are not.
2123.event: The hero destroys the king of karma and enters the city of no return.

claims.claim: liberation is an entry into a city from which there is no return

2124.reading: After the mind-maid's sword of meditation has burned the karmic kings, he throws it away, embraces the girl called முடிவு and enters the rich city to which one comes back no more.
2124.nuance: The sword is the same weapon as in 2115; here it is discarded, which means that even meditation is a means and not the goal. Liberation is pictured as marriage to a maiden named முடிவு, so release is described in the language of the bridegroom.
2124.event: The hero casts away the sword of meditation, embraces the girl called end and enters the city of no return.

claims.claim: meditation is a tool that is thrown away once the karma is burned
liberation is a city from which none returns

2125.reading: Casting off the coverings, the boundless one swallows the world and the non-world together and stands unmoving, with the maiden called end, in the shining state of release.
2125.nuance: சிவகதி here names the liberated state in a Jain poem and is not a claim about the god Siva; line 3 has a stray ங் (முடிவென்னும் ங்கொடியுந்) that is corrupt.
2125.event: The hero removes the coverings of karma, takes in all knowable things and stays in the state of release.

claims.claim: with the coverings removed the soul knows world and non-world at once and remains in release

2126.reading: After many praises and bows, the gods make a fire-offering, bathe in the nectar of the wheel of virtue, shine with joy and, praising, each go to his own place.
2126.nuance: The gods' fire-offering (வேள்வி, line 2) sits inside a Jain scene of worship; the verse does not say it is the Vedic sacrifice.
2126.event: The gods worship with a fire-offering, bathe in the nectar of the dharma wheel and return to their places.

2127.reading: After the field is lost and Death and Desire leave his side, he sees the truth by the pure light of full knowledge and, undimmed in heaven's worlds, becomes the crest-jewel of the world.
2127.nuance: சூளாமணி, the work's own title, is used here of the liberated one, so the poem names itself from this verse.
2127.event: Death and Desire flee, and the hero attains full knowledge and becomes the crest-jewel of the world.

claims.claim: full knowledge (kevala) sees the true thing and conquers Death and Desire

2128.reading: With karma gone, the gods praise his feet each day; Prajapati rules the Brahma world sweetly, and Tirumal of the discus guards the sea-bound earth.
2128.nuance: Prajapati and Tirumal are the princes of the epic's story; here they are shown ruling after the story's close, and the verse does not say whether Prajapati is the one who is liberated.
2128.event: The gods worship the liberated lord's feet while Prajapati rules Brahma's world and Tirumal rules the earth.

2129.reading: While the lord who is theirs sweetly rules the gods' world, Tirumal clears the earth of common rule, lifts a straight sceptre under the gods' guard, and lives while kings praise his feet.
2129.event: Tirumal rules the earth with a straight sceptre, protected by the gods and praised by kings.

claims.claim: a king guards the earth by a straight sceptre, and the gods protect him

2130.reading: The one white as a conch and the one blue as a jewel of the sea, with arms like pillars, bow with the whole world to the lord who won the deceiving karma and keep a daily festival under his lotus feet.
2130.nuance: Reading the white one and the dark one as the two brothers of the story is from the colours alone; the verse does not give their names.
2130.event: The two brothers and the whole world worship the lord who won karma, keeping a festival at his feet each day.

claims.claim: the one who has conquered karma is the object of the world's worship

links.note: 2111 shuts the five sense-gates of a fortress and posts guards; Naladiyar 59 names the five gates (body, mouth, eyes, nose, ears) and promises release to one who can guard and steer the craving that comes through them.
links.teaches: Guarding the senses is shown as one wall among several defences and not a lone act, so restraint looks like the start of a campaign and not its end.

gains.a: The gates, which the fortress leaves as an unnamed row, are named as the five organs through which craving enters.
gains.b: The rule that guarding the gates leads to release gains walls, armed guards and a mind kept within, so sense-restraint is pictured as part of a larger war.

links.note: 2113 has the lord ride the elephant of knowledge with a diamond goad that is awareness; Kural 24 guards the five with the goad of firmness.
links.teaches: The same goad turns from a means of guarding the senses to a means of driving the army that kills the karmic enemy.

gains.a: The goad is no longer a guard against the senses but a driver of an assault, which the couplet leaves out.
gains.b: The couplet's goad gains the elephant it only implies, and gains a battle for the elephant to carry the rider into.

links.note: 2115 has the lord draw the sword of unbroken meditation soaked in samadhi; Neelakesi 86 says that humans of the land of deeds see their dark karma leave by penance.
links.teaches: Both Jain epics say karma is removed by the ascetic's own effort, and one gives that effort a face as a sword.

links.note: 2117 kills anger and its fellows one after another in a fixed sequence; Siddhar 87 asks when anger, speech and action, the 'I' and the mind will die so that release can be reached.
links.teaches: The Jain epic gives a battle order for the passions where the Siddhar only longs for them to die all at once.

gains.a: The passions, which 2117 names but leaves as figures in a rout, are made into an ordered list the seeker must wait out, with the mind and the 'I' added at the end.
gains.b: The Siddhar's longing gains a plan, in which anger falls first and the others follow in turn, in place of a single wish for the end of all.

links.note: 2124 throws away the sword of meditation once the karmic kings are dead; Kural 350 says to cling to the clinging of the one who has none, so as to let clinging go.
links.teaches: A useful hold, whether the sword or the clinging to the unclinging one, is to be dropped at the end of its work.

gains.a: The throwing away of the sword gives the Kural's paradox of a last clinging a scene in which the tool is dropped and an entry follows.
gains.b: The couplet's holding that lets go gains a picture of the very moment the tool is dropped, and of what comes after, an embrace and a city.

links.note: 2124 has the liberated one embrace the maiden called முடிவு; Cintamani 3117 has the king embrace the maiden Kevala with unblinking eyes.
links.teaches: Both Jain epics speak of release as a bride, but the Soolamani's bride is the end of birth and the Cintamani's is knowledge.

links.note: 2125 has the freed soul swallow the world and non-world together once the coverings are gone; Cintamani 3082 has the hero swallow the three worlds and the world of non-world after the four enemy kings fall.
links.teaches: The same formula for omniscience appears in both Jain epics, and only the Soolamani names the removal of coverings as its cause.

links.note: 2125 places the liberated soul in the state called சிவகதி and wins it by its own meditation; Tirumanthiram 6 says apart from the Lord there is no hard penance that can achieve and no way into his city.
links.teaches: The two texts both speak of an unreturning state but disagree on whether penance alone reaches it or only the Lord opens the way.

gains.a: The state of release, which the Soolamani reaches by effort alone, is set against a view in which that effort is useless without the Lord.
gains.b: The claim that no penance achieves without him gains a rival case in which a hero wins release by his own meditation with no god acting.

links.note: 2127 has Death and Desire flee the hero who wins by full knowledge; Tirumanthiram 345 tells of burning Death in the fire of yoga at Kadavur.
links.teaches: Both texts have Death beaten, but one by a man's own knowledge and the other by a god's fire.

gains.a: Death's defeat, which the Soolamani gives to an ascetic's knowledge, is set against a defeat worked by the Lord.
gains.b: The yoga-fire gains a human counterpart who beats Death without any god, so the Kadavur tale is no longer the only way to beat Death.

links.note: 2127 calls the lord who has conquered his enemies the crest-jewel of the world; Soolamani 1 opens by praising the one who conquered the whole sum of his deeds and now stands as a shining form.
links.teaches: The close of the poem answers its opening, so the praise promised at the start is now earned by the war just fought.

links.note: 2130 shows the dark and white princes worshipping under the lotus feet of the liberated lord; Soolamani 2 says the story is of the one who in an earlier day went to him for refuge.
links.teaches: The refuge sought at the beginning becomes the festival of worship at the end, which gives the story a completed arc.

links.note: 2121 has the sky filled with the gods' regalia, flowers, sandal and powder; Cintamani 3090 has the gods rain flowers, coloured sandal and incense that fill the quarters.
links.teaches: The same festival of gods is set at the end of the war in the Soolamani and at the teaching in the Cintamani, so it honours victory in one and instruction in the other.

links.note: 2129 has Tirumal lift a straight sceptre with the gods guarding him; Kural 547 says the king guards the world and justice guards him if he does not falter.
links.teaches: The guard of a king comes in the epic from the gods and in the couplet from his own justice, so the pairing asks what really protects a ruler.

gains.a: The gods' protection, which the epic gives as a plain fact, is made to depend on the rule of a straight sceptre.
gains.b: The couplet's guard of justice gains a mythic setting in which the gods are the guards.

links.note: 2115 has samadhi give the sword that cuts the foe; Tirumanthiram 121 has the Siva-yogi cut bonds and remain with the body as if dead.
links.teaches: Samadhi is a weapon of conquest in the Jain epic and a quiet stillness in the Tirumanthiram, so the same state is used for opposite pictures.

gains.a: Samadhi gains an aggressive purpose, in which it is the sword, where the Tirumanthiram uses it for rest.
gains.b: The still, deathlike state gains a battle in which it is the weapon that ends the enemy.

source_issues: Verses 2123 to 2126 carry no build flags but 2123 line 1 (கருமால் வினையரசு காறளர நூறிப்து) and 2125 line 3 (a stray ங் in முடிவென்னும் ங்கொடியுந்) are corrupt, so those verses are marked uncertain.
Verses 2111 to 2122 and 2127 were printed as eight half-lines and joined into four by the build; 2130 had a stray pulli after a vowel sign removed.
The lord who wins release is not named in 2111 to 2130; the cast id hero_lord is inferred from கோன் in 2122 and 2127, and the verses do not say who he is.
